tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }

The page doesn't include scoring criteria or Claude Code-specific setup steps, so I've left those out. Commands are reproduced exactly as shown. Other instructions are paraphrased.

**1. Install the CLI**

```
# macOS/Linux:
curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash

# Windows:
irm https://entire.io/install.ps1 | iex
```

**2. Account signup and repo access**

- Sign in at entire.io with GitHub and authorize the Entire GitHub App when prompted. This can be done before or after importing the repo.
- A GitHub organization admin installs the Entire GitHub App on the organization through onboarding and imports the repository. Nothing appears for the team until this is done.
- Access follows the GitHub collaborator list. Changes can take up to an hour to sync. If the repo is missing, ask your org admin.

**3. Enable Entire in your repo and capture a session**

```
cd your-repo
entire enable
```

Start a new agent session, ask it for a focused change, and review the result.

**4. Commit and inspect the checkpoint**

```
git add path/to/changed-file
git commit -m "Build my first feature with Entire"
entire checkpoint list
entire checkpoint explain HEAD
```

When prompted, choose yes to link the commit to session context.

**5. Trails (feature-flagged)**

- Request access by filling in the Trails access form: https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/REDACTED/viewform
- After Entire enables it, open your repo in Entire, go to **Settings → General**, and turn on **Runners**, **Auto build on push**, and **Trails**. This requires repository admin permission.
- From the repo root, run `entire runner setup -y`, then commit and push the generated `.entire/` files.
- Create a Trail by asking your agent or running `entire trail create`. Then commit and push to the Trail branch as usual.

**6. Continuous Memory (optional): entire-graph**

```
entire plugin install graph
entire graph init-agents --repo .
entire graph stats --repo .
```

Commit `.entire/graph-agent.md`, `AGENTS.md`, and `CLAUDE.md`, then start a fresh agent session.

**7. Continuous Memory (optional): entire-brain**

Install from a prebuilt binary:

```
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/entireio/entire-brain/main/scripts/get-brain.sh | bash
```

Or build from source (requires Go 1.27+, Git 2.36+, the Entire CLI on your PATH, and a C compiler):

```
git clone https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain.git
cd entire-brain
./scripts/install.sh
```

Then, in your project repo:

```
entire brain setup
entire brain init-agents
entire brain mcp --print-config
claude mcp add entire-brain -- entire brain mcp
```

Commit the generated agent instructions (`.entire/agent-guide.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`) when they should apply to your team.

**8. Troubleshooting and docs for your agent**

```
entire doctor
entire doctor --force
claude mcp add --transport http entire-docs https://docs.entire.io/mcp
```

`entire doctor --force` fixes issues without prompting. For non-MCP setups, point your agent to https://docs.entire.io/llms.txt.

Atira Challenges is a platform for agent hackathons in industrial sales. Teams build an agent system that works through business software using any model via the platform's proxy.

**Challenge:** *From RFQ to bid.* The agent reads a public tender, finds the current specification, checks prices and stock in the ERP, looks up the approved discount in the sales inbox, and submits one signed bid.

**Setup**
- **Install the CLI:** `curl -fsSL https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/install.sh | sh` (Windows: `irm https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/install.ps1 | iex`). The CLI needs Node 24, or the installer offers a private copy.
- **Log in:** a team member runs `atira login`. `atira token` prints your personal token.
- **Authentication:** send the token or run token in an `x-api-key` header or as `Authorization: Bearer`. Plain HTTP and curl work; the API guide covers the device flow.
- **Coding agent integration:** `claude mcp add atira -- atira mcp` (Claude Code) or `codex mcp add atira -- atira mcp` (Codex). The MCP tools are `test_run`, `wait_for_run`, `diagnose_run`, `run_logs`, `run_screenshot`, `run_inputs`, and `submit`.
- **Local testing:** `atira scout --env` runs your agent locally against the public websites.
- **Starter kit:** `starter-kit.tar.gz`, a minimal Python skeleton with `agent.json` at the root. It covers reading the run, connecting to browsers over CDP, and calling hosted models.

**Submission**
- Submit your agent as a gzipped tarball.
- Each submission runs once on the public dataset (public-1), which feeds the leaderboard.

**Final evaluation**
- Each team's latest submission that passed review runs once on a private dataset. Teams can opt in before the final run starts to have it run best of three.
- The private dataset uses different websites, content, and data, so don't overfit to the public scenario.

**Scoring and ranking**
- Leaderboard order: eligible answers first, then higher quality, then lower cost × time.
- Winners are chosen by private-dataset performance, then public-dataset performance, then system elegance.

**Rules**
- The model must decide at run time where to go, what to search for, and which documents matter.
- Fixed scripts or crawlers that collect the websites for one model call are rejected in review.
- Values copied from the websites into the code are rejected.

**Not covered in this page:** deadlines, environment variables, the scouting logins, and the answer format and quality metrics. The page points to the Getting started guide, the API guide, the scoring doc, and the OpenAPI description for these.

# Atira starter kit

A minimal starting point, not an agent. It does the platform plumbing: it reads the run, attaches to the run's
browsers and shows how to call the free hosted models. Then it stops at `solve()` in `agent.py`, the place for your
agent. Out of the box it exits without an answer.

| File | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `run.py` | The run contract: reads the run (`load_run`) and submits an API answer (`submit_answer`) |
| `browsers.py` | Attaches to the run's browsers over CDP and gets a page (`connect`); locally it starts a Chromium |
| `models.py` | One call to each hosted model: `ask_qwen` (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next) and `ask_clef` (Cloudflare Clef) |
| `agent.py` | The entry point: reads the run, connects browser 1, calls `solve(task, page)` and submits what it returns |
| `agent.json` | How the sandbox installs (`uv sync`, the versions in `uv.lock`) and runs it; it waits for the hosted `qwen` |
| `tests/` | The plumbing against fakes |

## Your agent goes in `solve()`

`solve(task, page)` gets the run and a Playwright page in browser 1:

- `task["brief"]`: the task and its rules;
- `task["access"]`: each website's `siteId`, `url` and `credentials`;
- `task["submission"]`: where the answer goes, `{"kind": "api", "url": ...}` or `{"kind": "site", "url": ...}`;
- `task["answer_schema"]`: the JSON Schema of the answer.

For an `api` submission, return the answer and `main()` submits it: `202` is accepted and final, `400` lists the
issues to fix. For a `site` submission, enter the answer on that website yourself and return `None`. Reading pages,
acting on them and working out the answer are yours to build.

Mind the clock: a scored run has 20 minutes, and `run.seconds_left(task)` says how many seconds are left. Every part
of the answer scores on its own, so submit your best answer about a minute before the end rather than keep
searching; an answer that comes too late scores 0.

More browsers: set `"browsers": 2` (up to 4) in `agent.json`, then `await browsers.connect(playwright, 1)` attaches
to browser 2.

## The hosted models in short

Both are free and need no key of yours: runs get the variables, and locally `atira scout --env` sets them, pointed
at `atira models proxy`.

```python
import models

text = await models.ask_qwen("Which button submits this form? ...")          # QWEN_BASE_URL, QWEN_API_KEY
yes = await models.ask_clef({"page": page_text}, "Is this the current revision?")  # CLEF_BASE_URL, CLEF_API_KEY
```

`models.qwen()` is an OpenAI SDK client, for tool calls, images and everything else. Clef is set only where the
platform hosts it; if your agent relies on it, list `"models": ["qwen", "clef"]` in `agent.json` so the run waits for
it to warm up. Another provider works with your own key through the run's metering proxy:
`$API/docs/run-contract.md#llm-calls`.

## Run it locally

You need [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/) (open a new terminal after installing it, so
it is on your PATH) and the Atira CLI, signed in once with `atira login`.

Terminal 1: start the free models and leave it open.

```sh
atira models proxy
```

Terminal 2, in this folder:

```sh
uv sync && uv run playwright install chromium
eval "$(atira scout --env)"     # the scouting logins, and the model variables pointed at that proxy
uv run --no-sync python agent.py
```

In PowerShell on Windows, Terminal 2:

